analysis.one_liner: Makes agencies publish and publicly defend court settlements that set regulations, and delays most new rules six months.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 244-173 on an almost purely party-line vote on January 7, 2016; the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes how federal agencies settle lawsuits that force them to issue regulations. Before a court approves such a settlement, the agency would have to publish it 60 days in advance, take public comments, and certify that it approves any terms that commit the agency to a rulemaking deadline. Regulated companies and affected governments could intervene in the lawsuits and join the settlement talks. The bill also requires agencies to report monthly on upcoming rules, publish cost estimates, and post information about each rule online for six months before it can take effect, and it requires a plain-language 100-word summary of every proposed rule.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are the industries regulated by federal rules: they gain the right to intervene in lawsuits against agencies, presumptively join the settlement negotiations, comment on proposed settlements before they are filed, and see most new rules held back for six months while cost information is posted online. The public also gets some real benefits: settlements that set regulatory policy must be published in advance, agencies must explain the legal basis for them, and every proposed rule must come with a 100-word plain-language summary.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries, plus readers of rule summaries

how_it_helps.text: Requires an agency to publish any proposed consent decree or settlement that sets regulatory policy in the Federal Register and online 60 days before filing it with a court, accept public comments, and respond to them.

Lets parties affected by an agency action intervene in lawsuits against the agency, with a presumption that existing parties do not adequately represent them, and requires that interveners be included in settlement mediation.

Requires the Attorney General or an agency head to personally certify any settlement term that converts an agency's discretionary authority into a binding rulemaking deadline, commits unappropriated funds, or strips the agency of discretion.
Requires a court to give fresh ('de novo') review to a motion by an agency to modify an old settlement on the ground that it is no longer in the public interest.

Requires each agency to file monthly reports on every rule it expects to propose or finalize, with cost estimates and job-impact figures, and bars most rules from taking effect until the required information has been posted online for six months, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, criminal enforcement, national security, and trade-agreement rules.
Requires every proposed rule to include a plain-language summary of 100 words or less posted on regulations.gov.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the delay: rules on health, safety, the environment, and finance would sit for at least six months before taking effect, and lawsuits that push agencies to finish overdue rules would move more slowly because regulated parties can intervene and settlement terms face new hurdles. Advocacy groups that use litigation to compel agencies to act lose their main tool. Agencies bear added reporting and certification work.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public waiting on delayed protections

drawbacks.text: The six-month waiting period applies to essentially every rule, not just costly ones, so protections for health, safety, workers, and the environment would all be delayed together, with narrow exceptions only for emergencies, criminal enforcement, national security, and trade-agreement rules.

The intervention and mediation provisions give regulated companies a formal seat in lawsuits that public-interest groups bring to force agencies to act, letting the very parties the rules would constrain help shape or slow the settlement.

The comment period, certification requirements, and fresh judicial review of old settlements make it substantially harder for an agency to settle a lawsuit over delayed action, which can leave overdue regulations in limbo longer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces — published settlements, cost reporting, and 100-word plain-language summaries — are cheap and genuinely useful to the public. But the bill's center of gravity is procedural leverage for regulated parties: intervention rights in agency lawsuits and a six-month hold on nearly every rule. For readers, the honest trade is that you would see more about what agencies are doing, while the rules themselves — pollution limits, workplace and consumer protections — would arrive later.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on January 7, 2016 with Republicans almost unanimously in favor, but after it reached the Senate on January 11 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never heard from again, and it expired when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Collins (R-GA) introduced the bill on February 4, 2015, and all 22 of its cosponsors were Republicans.
The House Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 20 to 11 and reported it on June 25, 2015.
The House passed it on January 7, 2016 by 244 to 173, with 241 of 245 voting Republicans in favor and only 3 of 188 voting Democrats.
The Senate received the bill on January 11, 2016 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which took no further action before the 114th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agencies keep their existing ability to settle lawsuits over overdue rules without a 60-day pre-clearance process, and the advocacy groups that bring those lawsuits keep their main tool. Regulated industries do not get the intervention rights or the six-month hold on new rules they would have gained, and the public forgoes the bill's modest transparency additions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the groups that sue them

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 241 of 245 voting Republicans supported the bill and 173 of 188 voting Democrats opposed it; only 3 Democrats crossed over.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy, chemical, financial and other companies subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill gives these companies the right to intervene in lawsuits against agencies, presumptive seats in settlement talks, a 60-day comment window on proposed settlements, and a six-month hold on most new rules. That leverage slows the health, safety, environmental, and financial rules that would otherwise constrain them; the transparency titles cost them nothing.

industries.industry: Public-interest litigation groups (environmental, public health, and consumer advocates that sue agencies to compel rules)
industries.note: These groups' principal tool — negotiated consent decrees that set agency deadlines — would face a 60-day public pre-clearance process, intervention by regulated parties in the settlement itself, and new certification hurdles. Their lawsuits would take longer and settle on weaker terms.

The bill saddles agencies with monthly reporting, personal certifications, and longer timelines before rules take effect, but it also gives them a fresh avenue (de novo review) to modify old consent decrees they no longer want to follow.
